wolf-vs-goat.origin: Wolf vs Goat is an apparel brand, not a fiber, sheep breed or mill. Its public materials education discusses merino wool from the domestic sheep, Ovis aries, and named commercial yarns and cloths used in its garments. Fiber still originates on farms; spinning and weaving happen at mills the brand chooses to name in product stories. This atlas entry treats the brand as a teaching reference for materials language. It does not map commercial supply edges or certify any claim.
wolf-vs-goat.structure: Nothing in the brand name changes keratin chemistry. Merino wool remains alpha-keratin with cuticle scales, cortex and a mean fiber diameter measured in microns. When the brand discusses a mill yarn such as Zegna Baruffa's Cashwool, the yarn specification (for example a stated 19.5 micron extrafine merino in the mill's public description) is a commercial product grade, not a new generic fiber. Blends that add linen, cotton, silk or synthetics follow the chemistry of each component. Always read the garment's fiber content line for the legal composition.
wolf-vs-goat.process: Garment brands such as Wolf vs Goat typically buy dyed yarn or finished cloth, then cut and sew or fully fashion knitwear. The educational value of its public writing is the habit of naming stages: fiber diameter, spinner or weaver brand, and garment construction. Those stages remain separate. Australian or New Zealand merino may be spun in Biella-district mills and knitted elsewhere; a mill name is not a farm origin. Process claims on a product page should be read as producer-attributed storytelling unless third-party certificates are also provided.
wolf-vs-goat.performance: Performance belongs to the specified fiber, yarn and fabric, not to the apparel brand name. Fine merino near 19 to 20 microns is commonly comfortable for next-to-skin knitwear for many wearers, while coarser wool may prickle; mill finishing can change hand further. Dense multi-ply knits can improve durability and shape retention compared with lean singles of the same fiber, at the cost of weight. Producer phrases such as cashmere-like hand or zero pilling are marketing comparisons unless tied to a test method and a specific product. Evaluate abrasion, pilling and dimensional change from garment tests or wear, not from the brand alone.
wolf-vs-goat.identify: No laboratory test identifies Wolf vs Goat as a material. Microscopy and diameter measurement can characterize wool; selective dissolution and microscopy help confirm blends. Hangtags that name Cashwool, Afromood, Pecora Nera or similar mill products identify commercial yarn or cloth lines discussed by the brand, not generic fiber classes. Confusing a mill yarn brand with a species name, or assuming every micron story equals a Super S cloth number, is the common error this reference entry exists to prevent.
wolf-vs-goat.labeling: Wolf vs Goat is a trademark of an apparel company, not a generic fiber name under US 16 CFR Part 303 or Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. Labels must still state fibers and percentages, for example wool, or wool with silk and linen. Wool claims fall under the Wool Products Labeling Act and 16 CFR Part 300 in the United States. Mill yarn brands and fabric collection names are additional commercial designations; they do not replace generic fiber disclosure. Marketing education on a website is not a substitute for the sewn-in label.
wolf-vs-goat.past: Specialty menswear brands that teach fabric grammar in public have a long retail history, from swatch books to blog explainers. Wolf vs Goat's published product stories name mill yarns and talk through micron and construction in that tradition. This atlas records the brand as a reference lens on materials literacy. Corporate founding dates, ownership and factory lists should be taken from the company's current primary disclosures rather than guessed here.

canali.origin: Canali is an Italian menswear house, not a fiber, sheep breed or mill trademark for a keratin. Public materials and press language place the house in the Biella textile culture of northern Italy, where wool cloth for suiting is woven and finished. Fiber still originates on farms; spinning and weaving may occur at mills the house selects. This atlas entry is a teaching reference for Biella menswear vocabulary. It does not map commercial supply edges or certify any claim.
canali.structure: Nothing in the Canali name changes wool chemistry. Suiting cloth remains wool or a stated blend: alpha-keratin fibers, yarn twist, weave (for example warp-faced twills such as gabardine) and finish determine hand. Super S cloth numbers, if quoted on a cloth ticket, are commercial cloth designations rather than a farm micron certificate. Always read the garment fiber-content line for the legal composition.
canali.process: A menswear house typically specifies or buys finished cloth, then cuts and sews tailored garments. Biella provenance language refers to a district of mills and finishers, not to a single farm. Process stages to keep separate are farm fiber, spinning, weaving or knitting, dyeing or finishing, and make-up. Producer pages and cloth tickets are attributed stories; they are not atlas-invented logistics.
canali.performance: Performance belongs to the specified cloth and construction, not to the house name alone. Dense wool suiting can drape and crease differently from open tropical weaves; elastane blends change recovery. Weather or stain finishes apply only when documented for that cloth. Evaluate abrasion, seam strength and press retention from the garment and cloth specification, not from brand prestige.
canali.identify: No laboratory test identifies Canali as a material. Microscopy and diameter measurement characterize wool; selective tests help confirm blends. Hang tags and woven logos identify the garment brand. A Biella or Italy country-of-origin line identifies where a stage was performed, not necessarily where the sheep were raised.
canali.labeling: In the United States, wool products follow 16 CFR Part 300; in the EU, fiber names follow Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. The house name is a trademark, not a generic fiber name. Country-of-origin and care labels remain mandatory disclosures separate from marketing copy about Biella style or heritage.
canali.past: Canali’s public history is that of a twentieth-century Italian menswear house growing with Biella cloth culture. Exact founding anecdotes and ownership changes should be taken from the producer’s own chronology. The atlas uses the name to teach how garment houses, mill districts and fiber classes differ.
